analysis.one_liner: Speeds generic drug competition by limiting patent stays and forcing removal of invalidated patents.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to speed generic drug approval by limiting 30-month patent stays was introduced in July 2019, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug maker sues a generic competitor over patents, FDA approval of the generic is usually frozen for up to 30 months while the lawsuit plays out. This bill would limit that freeze to lawsuits over the core chemical compound itself, so patents on minor features like formulations or packaging could no longer delay a generic for years. It would also require the FDA to strike drug patents from its official list once the patent office has invalidated them. Together, these changes would let cheaper generic versions reach the market sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay for prescription drugs, including the millions who take brand-name drugs that face no generic competition. Faster generic entry typically pushes prices down sharply, often by 80% or more once multiple generic makers compete. Insurers and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid also save.

how_it_helps.text: Limits the 30-month automatic freeze on generic approval to lawsuits over patents that claim the drug's core compound, so weaker patents on drug products or methods of use can no longer stall a generic by default [S2][S3].

Requires drug makers to notify the FDA when the Patent Office has cancelled patent claims in an inter partes or post-grant review, and requires the FDA to strike those patents from the Orange Book list that generics must certify against [S2][S3].
Preserves the 180-day exclusivity reward for the first generic applicant even when a patent is stricken from the list, so the incentive to challenge bad patents stays intact [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, whose revenue from a single drug can depend on years of extra patent-protected exclusivity. They lose a tool that currently delays generic competition by default whenever they sue over any listed patent.

drawbacks.text: Limiting automatic stays to compound patents could weaken protection for genuine follow-on innovation, such as improved formulations that make a drug easier to take; brand makers argue those improvements deserve defense while the suit proceeds [S2].

The bill leaves the underlying patent litigation system in place, so brand companies could still sue over weaker patents; it only removes the automatic 30-month delay, and generic challengers would still bear the cost and risk of fighting those suits in court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is a targeted fix to a well-known delay tactic, and it preserves the first-filer exclusivity that drives patent challenges. The main cost is some reduced protection for incremental formulation improvements, but generic drugs with the same active compound treat the same disease just as well. The benefits to patients and payers are concrete; the costs fall almost entirely on brand-name manufacturers' future revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee and stayed there; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote ever happened before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley (R-WV) introduced the bill on July 17, 2019, joined by Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT) as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the next day to that committee's Health Subcommittee [S5].
No further action of any kind was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: the default 30-month delay tool survives intact, and patients kept paying the prices that come with delayed generic competition.

for.name: Rep. David McKinley
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit 30-month patent stays and require Orange Book updates for invalidated patents.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 17, 2019, sent it to the Health Subcommittee the next day, and never scheduled a hearing or markup in the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan, one Republican and one Democrat, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill removes two delay tools: automatic 30-month stays triggered by lawsuits over weak patents, and invalidated patents lingering on the FDA's Orange Book list. Every extra month of exclusivity protects brand-price revenue that comes out of patients' and insurers' pockets.

Generics could reach the market sooner because non-compound patent suits no longer freeze approval by default, and cleared patents must come off the Orange Book. The first-filer 180-day exclusivity reward is preserved [S3].
